Convolution as addition of supports

Reconstructed by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, 4 October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Adding two source locations explains both the power and the limitation of convolution. Two compact sources always give a distribution at their sums. Two unbounded sources do so when a bounded output can receive contributions only from a compact set of input pairs. This geometric condition will also control limits, associativity and local regularity.

Pairings are complex-linear, with no conjugation. We use U008, Proposition 1.2 and Theorem 5.1, for finite-order extensions and distributional limits; its formula (T1) characterizes bounded test families. The functional prerequisite, Sections 6 and 14.1–14.2, proves Baire's theorem and completeness of fixed-support test spaces. The scalar prerequisite, Sections 13.1–13.5 and 13.10, and the integration prerequisite, Sections 15.0–15.4, supply differentiation, compact cutoffs, ordinary integration and smooth approximation. All additional distribution constructions used below are proved here. The operator theorem also uses the exact Fourier inversion proof in the Schwartz prerequisite, F2–F4.

Pairings, parameters and tensor products

Write for an open subset of Euclidean space. For tests supported in a fixed compact set, write . A distribution is a linear form with a bound on each such space. A bounded test family has one common compact support and a uniform bound for every , by U008 (T1). Weak convergence means convergence on each test; strong convergence means uniform convergence on every bounded test family. The distinction concerns topologies even though U008 Theorem 5.1 proves that weakly convergent sequences also converge strongly.

B0. Localization and extended pairings. Define as the complement of the union of open sets where vanishes. It is closed, and whenever the compact support of misses it. Here is the localization step behind that assertion. Cover the compact support by finitely many open sets on which vanishes. Choose nonnegative smooth bumps supported in those sets with near the compact support, using smaller balls and the supplied cutoff construction. On that neighborhood divide by , and multiply by a compact cutoff supported there and equal to one near the test support. The smooth functions are extended by zero outside the region where the denominator is positive. They sum to one near the test support. Thus , and every summand pairs to zero. The same partition proves that compatible local distributions glue: evaluate a test by the finite sum of its partitioned local pairings; a common refinement proves independence, and a fixed finite partition near each compact gives continuity.

If and is compact in , set Two choices differ by a compact test whose support misses : at a point in their difference vanishes nearby, and at a point of the function vanishes nearby. B0 therefore proves independence. A common cutoff proves bilinearity whenever the finitely many relevant intersections are compact. Empty intersection gives zero. In particular a compactly supported distribution acts on every smooth function, with an estimate for one fixed cutoff. Multiplication by a smooth function and derivatives, defined by are distributions by the finite product rule and have support contained in that of . A compactly supported distribution consequently has some finite global order. We denote the space of compactly supported distributions by .

A continuous function which defines the zero distribution is zero pointwise. Otherwise multiply its value at a nonzero point by a constant complex phase to make its real part positive; continuity and a nonnegative bump of positive integral in a small neighborhood contradict the zero pairing. Associativity and continuity need support control

Theorem 3.1 (associativity). Let be nonempty closed envelopes of the supports of . Suppose that the preimage of every compact set under addition of triples in is compact. Then both iterated convolutions exist and Their common value on is the support-relative pairing of with . In particular, at least two compact factors suffice.

Proof. Fix . Pairs in with sum in a compact , together with third coordinate , lie in the compact triple preimage of . They form a closed subset, so pair addition is proper. Fixing a point of each other nonempty envelope gives the other pair properness statements. The sum is closed by Section 1. For a sequence whose sums lie in a compact set, choose . Triple properness gives a convergent subsequence of . Thus the pairs have a convergent subsequence; their relevant preimage is closed, so addition on is proper. This proves existence of both associations.

Here are the cutoffs that justify equality. Put . Choose a compact smooth cutoff equal to one near the preimage of in . In evaluating , the inner convolution involves only in the compact first projection of . Choose a compact cutoff near all pairs in with sums in that projection, using pair properness. Formula (1.7), B1 and the iterated tensor identity give the compact triple pairing This test is compact: lies in , and in the second projection of . Its cutoff multiplier is one near every contributing point of the triple support with sum in . B0 identifies it with the canonical extended triple pairing. Repeating the same construction for the other association gives the same pairing, by B2's tensor associativity.

If two factors are compact, choose nonempty compact envelopes for them, using for a zero factor, and any nonempty closed envelope for the third. Bounded sums and bounded first two coordinates bound the third. Closedness then proves triple properness.

The nonempty-envelope hypothesis addresses an actual intermediate-existence issue. An empty envelope forces its distribution to be zero. The canonical triple pairing is then zero, and every association whose inner convolution is defined is also defined and zero. It does not define an otherwise missing inner convolution. For example, , , and have a proper empty triple preimage. The association is zero, whereas has no inner convolution under this construction, as (3.5) shows.

For , , , the theorem gives Indeed both are compact distributions. Differentiation under the ordinary compact integral makes smooth. The left side is also a smooth function, by compact integration of the smooth against . The distributional identity therefore holds pointwise by B0. Lemma 2.2 justifies the interchanges even for merely continuous .

Theorem 3.2 (continuity with fixed support sets). On fixed closed where addition is proper, convolution is separately continuous in both the weak and strong distribution topologies. If , are weakly convergent sequences supported in , then weakly.

Proof. A limit has the designated support because every test in its complement has zero pairing with each term. For a fixed output test, use one cutoff in (1.7). Separate weak continuity is then B3. A bounded family of output tests has common compact support , so one such cutoff works for the whole family. Product and chain rules show that is bounded in the product test space. B3 proves separate strong continuity. Its joint sequence conclusion (B7), applied to each such fixed compact test, proves joint weak convergence.

The support constraint cannot be dropped: The two inputs eventually miss each compact test support, but their sum stays at zero.

Proof. For any fixed number of contributing coordinates, suppose their sums remain bounded while their maximum norm tends to infinity. All these additions are proper. Also by closedness and scaling, and . Theorems 1.1 and 3.1 give closure, commutativity, associativity and the identity. Translation-invariant operators have one convolution kernel

We first prove the two kernel facts needed for the operator theorem.

K1. Constructing a kernel from a separately continuous pairing. Suppose is a complex bilinear form on which is continuous in each variable with the other fixed. There is a unique satisfying .

Fix compact supports . On the complete metric space , form the closed sets They are closed because is continuous for each . Their union is the space: continuity of gives one finite-order bound for each fixed , and increasing bounds its order and constant. The complete-space and Baire proofs are in the functional prerequisite, Sections 6 and 14.1–14.2. Thus some contains . Subtract the inequality at from that at , and then rescale . Since includes the zeroth derivative, it is zero only for the zero test. This gives Specifically works. This is the joint estimate we need; separate continuity alone was the hypothesis.

Choose compact smooth cutoffs equal to one on neighborhoods of two given closed boxes, and apply (K1) with their supports. Put . The Schwartz prerequisite F2–F4 proves the Fourier convention and inversion Define The second factor depends continuously on the frequencies: the compact exponential tests depend continuously on them in every derivative seminorm, and (K1) controls the change in either argument of . This is an absolutely convergent scalar integral. Indeed (K1) bounds that factor by . For on any fixed compact support, integration by parts from F2 gives Choose . The product of these bounds is integrable: on its integral is bounded by a constant times , whose sum is geometric, and the unit ball has finite volume. Thus has a finite test seminorm bound and is a distribution.

For , Fubini gives . Fourier inversion and (K1) show To justify the passage through , truncate the frequency integrals to boxes and approximate by Riemann sums. Every derivative of grows at most polynomially in ; the rapid decrease of bounds the tails in every test seminorm on the one fixed support . The same holds for . The truncated sums therefore converge in the fixed-support test spaces, and the bound (K1) permits both limits. This proves (K4) without a vector-valued integration theorem.

On tests supported inside the boxes where both cutoffs are one, this distribution is independent of the cutoffs: by B2 approximate such a test by finite product sums supported within those boxes, and use (K4) for each sum. Choose increasing boxes exhausting each Euclidean space. The resulting distributions agree on the smaller product boxes by this argument. For an arbitrary compact test choose one containing product box and use its functional; agreement proves independence and linearity, while its finite bound proves continuity. This constructs . Product-test density B2 proves uniqueness. No growth condition on outside fixed compact supports has been imposed.

  • Richard Melrose, 18.155 Lecture 15: Schwartz's kernel theorem, freely accessible MIT lecture, 1 November 2016. Pages 2–4 explain separate continuity, the Baire estimate and localization by cutoffs. The kernel construction here uses the supplied Fourier inversion proof and the explicit integral (K2); it does not require the lecture's additional Sobolev-space machinery.

Every distributional construction and operator identity used above has its proof here or at one of the exact programme locations listed. The freely accessible human texts support the construction of these proofs.
